summary.summary: This is the REVISED, pre-approval version of Appendix A to North Northamptonshire's 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement (AGS), going to the Audit and Governance Committee. The Council judges its governance arrangements generally effective, providing a moderate level of assurance, with 71% of 13 tracked 2024/25 governance actions implemented during the year (page 21); the rest — timely closure of internal-audit actions, social-care/DSG financial sustainability, consistent safeguarding controls, and assurance over shared services/partnerships — carry forward as live risks for 2026/27. It notes an overall revenue overspend against the 2025/26 budget in demand-led adults' and children's social care, partially offset by earmarked reserves, though no monetary figures are given in this narrative document (page 9). Against the Draft appendix (queue E06000061-7f338f1e), this REVISED copy adds one short paragraph on the Corporate Scrutiny Committee's review of performance/budget-monitoring reports (page 9) but is otherwise near-identical in substance.

compliance.notes: Scored from the complete Executive pack of 10 February 2026 (TMSS cover report plus Appendices A-E) together with the General Fund Final Budget/MTFP/Capital Programme report and its Budget Book, which carries the Capital Investment Strategy at pp.111-131. The Council HAS a Housing Revenue Account — Appendix B para 5.18 describes HRA self-financing for the legacy Kettering and Corby stock with loans assigned to one fund or the other and an Item 8 charge between the General Fund and the HRA; Appendix C charges no MRP on HRA assets and budgets £1.000m of HRA loan repayment; para 6.1 budgets £3.3m of HRA debt interest; and the capital programme includes £61.665m of HRA capital expenditure. HRA-conditional requirements were therefore scored as applicable, and the Council is marked down on two of them (no separate HRA liability benchmark, LB-04; and a General-Fund-only financing-costs ratio with no HRA equivalent, PI-07). Strongest areas by some distance: the liability benchmark (Table 2 plus an Arlingclose chart to 2075 with all four balances), the treasury investment strategy and counterparty framework, and governance/practices — Appendix E is a full 62-page TMP1-TMP12 document with schedules, a role-by-role dealing authorisation matrix and named external providers, which most authorities never publish. Weakest area: the non-treasury/commercial family in the 5-page Appendix D, where proportionality is recited but never demonstrated, no ratio of commercial income to net revenue stream is produced, no monetary limit caps commercial property investment, and the specified/non-specified analysis is inconsistent with the long-dated instruments the TMSS approves. The separate HRA Budget 2026-27 report was not in the pack but suppresses nothing scored here.

gaps.evidence: Appendix B p.11 para 5.11 table and Budget Book p.131 Table 11: financing costs £10.4m/£10.1m/£10.1m/£10.0m/£9.9m; proportion of net revenue stream 2.96% / 2.33% / 2.18% / 2.05% / 1.89% (2025/26 forecast to 2029/30)

Appendix E TMP6 p.39 lists 'Net income from commercial and service investments to net revenue stream' among the prudential indicators the Council will cover in its annual strategy documents; Appendix D p.5 Table 5 gives rates of return (commercial property 4.69%) but not as a ratio to the net revenue stream

Appendix E TMP3 p.25 and Appendix B para 3.14 restate the substance of Prudential Code paras 51–53 (no borrowing to invest primarily for financial return; PWLB certification), but no document contains a compliance statement citing paragraphs 51 to 53

Cover report para 4.6 and Appendix E TMP3 p.24 recite the principle that 'the risks of the Council's commercial investments should be proportionate to the Council's overall capacity — ie that plausible losses could be absorbed in budgets or reserves without unmanageable detriment to local services'; Appendix D para 3.2 sets service-loan limits 'to ensure that total exposure to service loans remains proportionate to the size of the Council'; Appendix D p.5 Table 4 gives total investment exposure of £157.896m (31.3.25) falling to £34.691m (31.3.27)

Appendix D p.2 Table 1 approved limits on service loans — subsidiaries £2.000m, local businesses £1.000m, local charities £0.500m, employees £0.500m, other £0.500m; p.3 Table 2 approved limit on shares in subsidiaries £2.000m

findings.headline: Sponsored academy conversions leave deficits with the local authority to be funded from core budget; converter academies take their deficits.
findings.detail: When a school with a deficit converts to a sponsored academy, the deficit remains with the council and is funded from the council's core budget. When it becomes a converter academy, the deficit transfers to the academy. This distinction creates ongoing exposure when sponsored conversions occur.
findings.matters: A lender assessing contingent liabilities needs to understand that sponsored academy conversions can leave the council funding unresolved school deficits.
findings.figures: No limits on sponsored academy deficit transfer specified
findings.quote: Where a school with a deficit is to open as a sponsored academy, the deficit remains with the LA, to be funded from its core budget.

findings.headline: Licensed school deficits capped individually at 15 per cent of budget share and collectively at 10 per cent of total maintained school balances.
findings.detail: Deficits of 1 per cent or more trigger a requirement for formal recovery plans. Individual licensed deficits are capped at 15 per cent of a school's budget share and must be recovered within three years from the start of the next financial year. Across all schools, the council will not permit total deficit arrangements to exceed 10 per cent of its collective maintained school balances.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's maximum risk tolerance for school deficits; a peer council can benchmark its own thresholds.
findings.figures: 1% trigger for recovery plan requirement; 15% maximum per school; 10% maximum collectively; 3-year recovery period
findings.quote: The maximum proportion of the collective school balances held by the Council which will be used to back the total of deficit arrangements is 10%.

findings.headline: Council explicitly underwriting school bank overdrafts and charging interest costs back to the school's budget.
findings.detail: Where a school's bank account goes into overdraft, the council will underwrite it, but the school's budget bears the interest and other costs incurred. This creates direct financial exposure for the council to school cash management failures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council has accepted direct liability for school overdraft costs, not just future deficit recovery.
findings.figures: No limits specified on overdraft exposure
findings.quote: where an unplanned overdraft occurs on a school's local bank account, although the Council will underwrite such an overdraft, the school's budget will be charged any interest or other costs that arise.

findings.headline: Council cannot write off school deficits; they remain permanent liabilities recovered through deduction from following years' budget shares.
findings.detail: The policy states the council cannot write off school deficits. All shortfalls must be carried forward year to year, deducted from the following year's budget share, creating a permanent liability until schools recover them. Schools are not permitted to budget for a deficit except in exceptional circumstances with council agreement.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's exposure needs to understand it has accepted a permanent liability for school deficits that only schools themselves can resolve.
findings.figures: No quantification given in this policy document
findings.quote: The Council cannot write off the deficit balance of any school.

findings.paper_title: 5.Proposed 0.5% Schools Block Transfer to High Needs Block
findings.headline: Council proposing 0.5% Schools Block transfer to High Needs Block for 2027-28, repeating 2026-27 transfer of £1.617m
findings.detail: In 2026-27 Schools Forum agreed a 0.5% transfer of £1.617m to fund early intervention and targeted support. The council is now seeking approval in principle for a similar transfer for 2027-28. Transfers up to 0.5% require school forum approval; amounts above this threshold require Secretary of State approval.
findings.matters: Repeating an annual transfer indicates the council is managing escalating SEND demand through targeted intervention; the transfer supports schools to meet needs without immediate reliance on statutory EHCPs.
findings.quote: In 2026-27 Schools Forum agreed to transfer of 0.5% from the Schools Block funding, amounting to £1.617m. North Northamptonshire Council is now seeking the Schools Forum's agreement in principle for a similar transfer for the 2027-28 financial year.
